title:
Systems &
scaling
intro: Phase 1 taught you to build a model. This phase teaches you to run one at a size that does not fit on a single device, and to serve one fast enough that an eval loop can hammer it. You start with four weeks of JAX at reading depth — enough to follow a scaling-book snippet or a Gemma reference implementation without getting stuck on tracing rules. Then two weeks of framework-agnostic scaling arithmetic: rooflines, arithmetic intensity, sharding cost models, and what Chinchilla actually claimed versus what people quote. The back half is PyTorch and it is where you spend the money: FSDP2 and DTensor, CS336 assignment 2 with a FlashAttention kernel in Triton, and finally vLLM and SGLang. Serving is not a detour. Every eval you write in Phase 3 and every RL rollout you generate runs behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and if you cannot debug that endpoint you cannot debug your own results.

callouts.html: Budget the compute before week 21. Weeks 27–34 need real multi-GPU time. A 2×A100 or 2×L40S box on a spot market is enough for FSDP2, tensor parallel and vLLM tensor-parallel serving; you do not need eight H100s. Expect $150–400 across this phase. Set a hard cap, use spot, and kill instances the moment a run ends.

items.title: Purity and the tracing model
items.desc: Read "How to think in JAX." JAX transforms require pure functions — no side effects, no in-place mutation, no Python state captured across calls. Then deliberately cause the three failure modes: a leaked tracer, an in-place mutation that silently does nothing, and a Python `if` on a traced boolean. Knowing the error text on sight is the entire point of this item.

items.title: grad, value_and_grad, and jit
items.desc: Work `jax.grad` over a loss and a parameter pytree, then `value_and_grad` so you are not recomputing the forward pass. For jit, the thing to internalise is the cache key: shapes and dtypes. A shape change recompiles; a Python value passed as an argument recompiles every call unless you mark it `static_argnums`. Time the first call and the second call separately — the delta is compile cost.

items.title: vmap
items.desc: vmap turns a single-example function into a batched one by rewriting the computation, not by looping. Build the canonical pattern — `vmap(grad(loss))` for per-example gradients — and one pairwise-distance function where broadcasting by hand would be error-prone. Learn what `in_axes` and `out_axes` do, because you will read them constantly.

items.title: lax.scan and structured control flow
items.desc: A Python for-loop inside jit unrolls: N iterations become N copies of the graph and compile time explodes. `lax.scan` compiles one iteration and loops inside XLA. Write a scan-based training step with `carry = (params, opt_state)` and metrics accumulated in the outputs. Also build one working `lax.cond` and one `lax.while_loop` so you recognise them in other people's code.

items.title: Explicit sharding and meshes
items.desc: Explicit sharding has been the default since JAX 0.9.0: `jax.make_mesh` builds meshes with `AxisType.Explicit`, shardings propagate through the type system, and ambiguous communication is an error rather than something the compiler silently inserts. Activate a mesh with `jax.set_mesh(mesh)` — bare `with mesh:` was deprecated in 0.10.1 — and annotate arrays with `jax.P`, the top-level PartitionSpec alias. Write one step that replicates parameters and shards the batch along the data axis.

items.title: Collectives and shard_map
items.desc: `lax.psum` and `lax.pmean` are AllReduce with a name on the mesh axis; every parallelism strategy in the scaling book reduces to placing these correctly. `jax.shard_map` is manual mode — you write the per-device program and place the collectives yourself. Use the top-level `jax.shard_map`, not the old `jax.experimental.shard_map` import. Since 0.9.1, under Explicit mode shard_map asserts your input spec matches `in_specs` instead of resharding for you, so call `jax.reshard` first when they differ.

items.title: Read pmap, never write it
items.desc: Almost every JAX tutorial, blog post and older scaling-book snippet you will find is built on `pmap`. JAX 0.10.0 removed the C++ pmap infrastructure; `jax.pmap` survives only as a thin wrapper over `jit(shard_map)`, and `PmapSharding`, `device_put_sharded` and `device_put_replicated` now raise AttributeError. Skim the changelog for the removals so you can date any snippet you find, then translate pmap code mentally into meshes and specs.

items.title: Get devices without a budget
items.desc: Colab no longer hands out TPU slices. Kaggle still offers free TPU time and is where the scaling book now points readers; a small GCP slice is the paid fallback. For everything in this task you do not need real accelerators at all — `jax.config.update("jax_num_cpu_devices", 8)` before the first JAX call gives you eight fake devices, which is enough for every mesh, sharding and shard_map exercise here and costs nothing. Verify `jax.devices()` and record what you actually ran on.

callouts.html: This is literacy depth on purpose. The roles you are targeting are overwhelmingly PyTorch, so shipping JAX is not the goal — reading it is. You need to open a scaling-book snippet, a MaxText training step or a Gemma reference implementation and know what it does. The concepts transfer directly: a JAX mesh is a PyTorch DeviceMesh, `jax.P` is a DTensor placement, `shard_map` is what `parallelize_module` generates for you, and psum/pmean is the NCCL AllReduce underneath FSDP2. Learn the vocabulary here and weeks 27–29 cost you half as much.

Do not build a JAX/Flax transformer. The old version of this plan rebuilt the model in Flax and did a deep dive on NNX and Optax. Both are cut. You built the transformer once in CS336 assignment 1 and that is the one that counts. Rebuilding it in a framework you will not ship in buys nothing an interviewer can check.

items.title: Chapters 1–2: rooflines and the hardware
items.desc: Chapter 1 is the single highest-value thing in this phase: FLOPs versus bytes moved, arithmetic intensity, and the question "is this operation compute-bound or memory-bound?" answered with arithmetic instead of a profiler. Chapter 2 grounds it in real accelerator numbers. Do the exercises with pencil and paper before you look at the answers.

items.title: Chapters 3–4: sharding and transformer math
items.desc: Chapter 3 gives you the cost model for every sharding strategy — what each one communicates, when it is worth it, and where it stops scaling. Chapter 4 counts the parameters, FLOPs and activation memory of a transformer forward and backward pass. Be able to derive the 6ND training-FLOP estimate and say exactly which terms it ignores and when ignoring them becomes wrong.

items.title: Chapter 12: how to think about GPUs
items.desc: This chapter did not exist when the book was first written and it is the one covering hardware you can actually rent. NVIDIA memory hierarchy, NVLink versus InfiniBand, collectives cost on a GPU fabric, and a direct GPU-versus-TPU comparison. Read it immediately before Task 03 — it is the bridge between the arithmetic and FSDP2.

resource.label: Scaling book — how to think about GPUs ↗

items.title: Chinchilla as the anchor
items.desc: Read the original compute-optimal paper and extract the actual claim: for a fixed training-compute budget, parameters and tokens should scale roughly in proportion, about 20 tokens per parameter. Then note the two things it does not say — it says nothing about inference cost, and it assumes unlimited unique data. Every later result in this item attacks one of those two assumptions.

items.title: Inference-aware and data-constrained scaling
items.desc: Read arXiv 2401.00448, which redoes the optimisation with inference demand in the objective and finds that if you will serve a lot of tokens, you should train a smaller model on far more data than Chinchilla says. Then read arXiv 2305.16264 on the data-constrained regime: repeated epochs decay in value, and there is a point past which more compute on repeated data buys nothing. Together these explain why every 2025–2026 open model is trained well past 20 tokens per parameter.

items.title: The GPU counterpart
items.desc: Hugging Face's Ultra-Scale Playbook is the PyTorch-side twin of the scaling book: 5D parallelism, ZeRO stages, activation recomputation, kernel fusion, all grounded in thousands of experiments up to 512 GPUs. Read the parallelism and memory chapters now and keep the tab open through Task 03 — it names the exact failure modes you are about to hit.

callouts.html: No LaTeX write-up, no screen recordings. The old plan had you typeset your derivations and record yourself solving problems. Both were theatre — nobody reads them and they cost a week. The deliverable here is that you can size a training run out loud: given a model, a batch size and a cluster, state the memory per device, whether you are compute- or bandwidth-bound, and what the step time should be. Test it by predicting a number before every run in Task 03 and writing down how wrong you were.

items.title: FSDP2
items.desc: FSDP2 (`fully_shard`) is the current API and it is not a rename of FSDP1 — it shards on dim-0 into DTensors instead of flattening parameters into a single per-rank buffer, which makes per-parameter state, mixed precision and checkpointing all behave sanely. Wrap a model from Phase 1, run it on two GPUs, and watch memory before and after. Understand what gets all-gathered in forward, what gets reduce-scattered in backward, and why wrapping granularity changes both.

items.title: DTensor and DeviceMesh
items.desc: DTensor is the substrate everything else in modern PyTorch distributed is built on: a tensor plus a DeviceMesh plus placements (Shard, Replicate, Partial). This is the direct analogue of the JAX mesh and PartitionSpec work you did in Task 01, so build the mapping explicitly. Construct a 2D mesh, place a tensor, redistribute it, and read the collectives that PyTorch inserts to make the redistribution happen.

items.title: Tensor parallel and 2D parallelism
items.desc: Tensor parallel splits individual matmuls across devices — column-wise then row-wise through an MLP block so only one all-reduce is needed per block. Apply `parallelize_module` with a ColwiseParallel/RowwiseParallel plan to your transformer, then compose it with FSDP2 on a second mesh axis for 2D parallelism. Measure the step time at TP=2 versus data parallel at the same device count and explain the difference from the chapter 3 cost model.

items.title: Read torchtitan
items.desc: torchtitan is where PyTorch consolidated its reference training stack — FSDP2, TP, pipeline parallel, float8, distributed checkpointing and compile, in a codebase small enough to read end to end. Read the parallelism configuration and the training loop closely. This is the repo to point at when someone asks how you would set up a real pretraining run, and torchtune's wind-down means it is now the only PyTorch-blessed answer.

items.title: Activation checkpointing and gradient accumulation
items.desc: These are the two levers that trade compute for memory, and you should know the arithmetic for both. Activation checkpointing drops stored activations and recomputes them in backward — roughly 30% more compute for a large memory cut; selective checkpointing keeps the expensive-to-recompute ops. Gradient accumulation buys a larger effective batch at zero memory cost but needs `no_sync` under FSDP or you pay for a reduce on every microbatch. Measure both, do not assume.

items.title: bf16 and fp8
items.desc: bf16 is the default training dtype because it keeps fp32's exponent range and therefore does not need loss scaling; know why fp16 does. Then go one step further with torchao's float8 training — per-tensor scaling, which layers are safe to cast, and what the measured speedup actually is on your hardware versus the marketing number. Run one training job in each precision on identical data and compare loss curves, not just throughput.

items.title: NCCL and OOM debugging
items.desc: Distributed jobs fail in two characteristic ways and you need both playbooks. For hangs: `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, `TORCH_NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING`, and the observation that a hang is almost always a collective that one rank did not reach. For OOM: read the CUDA memory snapshot, distinguish fragmentation from genuine exhaustion, and know that the peak is usually in backward, not forward. Deliberately cause a rank-divergence hang and a fragmentation OOM so you have seen both.

items.title: Distributed checkpoint and resume
items.desc: A training run you cannot resume is a training run you cannot afford. Use `torch.distributed.checkpoint` to save sharded state, then prove it: kill the job mid-epoch, restart it on a different world size, and verify the loss curve continues rather than jumping. Resharding on resume is the part that breaks, which is exactly why you test it.

callouts.html: Two GPUs beat zero GPUs by more than eight beat two. Nearly every bug in this task — wrong wrapping granularity, a collective one rank skips, a resharded checkpoint that will not load — reproduces at world size 2. Rent the smallest multi-GPU box you can find, debug there, and only scale up when the thing already works.

items.title: Watch the systems lectures
items.desc: CS336's lecture material covers kernels, profiling, GPU architecture and distributed training in the order the assignment needs them. Watch the systems block before writing any code — the assignment assumes the lecture content and will otherwise cost you days. Slides and executable lecture code are in the course repo.

items.title: Benchmark and profile before optimising
items.desc: Time the forward pass, the backward pass and a full optimizer step separately, with proper CUDA synchronisation and warmup iterations — an unsynchronised timing is measuring queue submission, not work. Then profile with the PyTorch profiler and read the trace: kernel time versus gaps, memory traffic, where the launch overhead lives. Write down a predicted number from your chapter 1 roofline before each measurement.

items.title: Triton fundamentals
items.desc: Triton lets you write a fused kernel in Python with block-level rather than thread-level semantics. Work the official tutorials in order — vector add, fused softmax, matmul — before attempting attention, because the softmax one teaches the exact online-normalisation trick FlashAttention depends on. Understand block pointers, masking for ragged tails, and `tl.load`/`tl.store` with boundary checks.

items.title: FlashAttention-2 forward and backward in Triton
items.desc: This is the hard part of the assignment and the part worth doing. Write the tiled forward with online softmax so the full attention matrix never materialises, then the backward pass, then check both against a naive PyTorch reference to tight tolerance. Benchmark against the reference across sequence lengths and show the crossover point where tiling starts to win. You wrote the paper's summary in Phase 1; now you write the kernel.

items.title: DDP from scratch, then optimizer state sharding
items.desc: Implement data-parallel training yourself on top of raw collectives: broadcast the initial parameters, all-reduce gradients after backward, and then improve it by bucketing gradients so communication overlaps with the backward pass instead of following it. Then shard the optimizer state (ZeRO stage 1) and measure the memory saved. Having built this by hand is what makes FSDP2's behaviour in Task 03 stop being magic.

callouts.html: Partial credit is the plan, not the fallback. Two weeks is tight for this assignment. Rank it: benchmarking and profiling first, then DDP with overlap, then the Triton forward, then the Triton backward. A green forward kernel with honest benchmarks and a written note on what defeated the backward pass is a better artifact than a silently abandoned repo. Commit the failure notes.

items.title: Stand up vLLM
items.desc: Serve a small open model with `vllm serve` and hit it through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Get comfortable with the knobs that actually matter: `--max-model-len`, `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-num-seqs`, and the engine's startup log where it reports how many KV cache blocks it allocated. Everything else in this task is a variation on this server.

items.title: Continuous batching and paged KV cache
items.desc: Static batching wastes the GPU whenever sequences in a batch finish at different times; continuous batching admits new requests at every decode step instead. PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks with an indirection table, which is what makes that admission cheap and eliminates the fragmentation of contiguous per-sequence allocation. Read how blocks are allocated, shared and evicted — preemption under memory pressure is a real behaviour you will have to explain when throughput collapses.

items.title: Read the PagedAttention paper
items.desc: The original vLLM paper is short and states the problem cleanly: KV cache memory, not compute, is what bounds serving throughput for LLMs, and pre-allocating contiguous cache for the maximum sequence length wastes most of it. Read it for the framing and the memory accounting, which carry over to every serving system that came after.

items.title: Prefix caching
items.desc: Automatic prefix caching hashes KV blocks so requests sharing a prefix reuse them instead of recomputing. This is the single largest win available to eval and RL workloads, where hundreds of samples share one long system prompt and few-shot block. Measure it: run the same eval batch with prefix caching on and off and record time-to-first-token and total throughput. That measured delta is a number worth putting in a writeup.

items.title: Tensor-parallel and multi-GPU serving
items.desc: Serving a model too large for one card means `--tensor-parallel-size`, and possibly pipeline parallel across nodes. Understand what this buys and what it costs: TP splits the weights and the KV cache so you get more cache headroom as well as more compute, but adds an all-reduce per layer, so latency improves sub-linearly. Run the same model at TP=1 and TP=2 and compare tokens/second per GPU, not just tokens/second.

items.title: Throughput versus latency, measured
items.desc: Build a small load generator and sweep concurrency, recording time-to-first-token, inter-token latency and total output tokens/second at each level. You will see the shape everyone talks about: throughput rises with concurrency until the KV cache saturates, while per-request latency degrades from the first request onward. Know where your endpoint's knee is, because Phase 3 eval runs will sit right on it.

items.title: Quantization
items.desc: Quantization is the cheapest way to fit a bigger model or a bigger KV cache on the hardware you have. Learn the distinctions that matter in practice: weight-only versus weight-and-activation, FP8 versus INT8 versus 4-bit, and KV-cache quantization as a separate decision from weight quantization. Serve one model at bf16 and one quantized, and evaluate both on the same task — the accuracy cost is workload-dependent and you should measure yours rather than quote a blog post.

items.title: Speculative decoding
items.desc: A small draft model, or n-gram lookup, or a self-speculation head proposes several tokens; the target model verifies them in one forward pass and accepts the longest correct prefix. Output is distributionally identical to normal decoding, so it is a pure latency win — but only when the acceptance rate is high and the batch is small, which means it can hurt a throughput-bound eval run. Enable it, measure acceptance rate and end-to-end latency, and know when to turn it off.

items.title: SGLang and structured generation
items.desc: SGLang is the other serving engine you should be able to speak to. Its distinguishing pieces are RadixAttention — a prefix tree over the KV cache that generalises prefix caching to arbitrary shared prefixes, which matters for branching agent traces — and fast constrained decoding for JSON and grammar-constrained output. Serve the same model on SGLang, run your load generator against it, and be able to say which engine you would pick for an agentic eval and why.

items.title: Wire the endpoint to an RL and eval harness
items.desc: Close the loop that motivates this whole task. Prime Intellect's `verifiers` library assumes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint backed by vLLM, so point it at the server you just built and run a trivial rollout. You are not learning the library yet — that is Phase 3 — you are proving the plumbing works and seeing where the endpoint becomes the bottleneck in a rollout loop.

callouts.html: This is the task that makes Phase 3 possible. Every eval you write and every RL rollout you generate goes through a served endpoint. When an eval run is inexplicably slow, when throughput collapses at sample 400, when two runs of the same eval disagree — the cause is usually the serving layer, not your harness. Owning this layer is also what separates an evals engineer from someone who calls an API.

milestone.title: Phase 2 complete
milestone.heading: What you ship at end of Phase 2
items: SHIP: You can read a JAX training step — mesh, jax.P annotations, shard_map, psum — and explain what each device holds and what crosses the interconnect, without writing JAX yourself
SHIP: You can spot pmap-era code on sight and say why it no longer runs on JAX 0.11
SHIP: Written scaling-book answers for chapters 1–4 and 12, in your repo as plain notes — including the ones you got wrong and the corrected working
SHIP: Given a model size, batch size and cluster, you can predict memory per device and step time on paper, and you have a log of predictions versus measured reality
SHIP: A working FSDP2 + tensor-parallel training run on a rented multi-GPU box, with a checkpoint that resumes correctly at a different world size
SHIP: A debugging writeup covering one NCCL hang and one OOM you caused deliberately, with the diagnosis and the fix

SHIP: CS336 assignment 2 in your repo — benchmarking and profiling complete, DDP with gradient bucketing built from scratch, and a Triton attention kernel benchmarked against the PyTorch reference (partial credit stated honestly)
SHIP: A vLLM endpoint you configured yourself, with a measured throughput-versus-latency curve, a measured prefix-caching speedup on a repeated-prompt workload, and a TP=1 versus TP=2 comparison
SHIP: A short comparison of vLLM and SGLang with a stated pick for agentic eval workloads and the reason
SHIP: `verifiers` running a rollout against your own endpoint — the plumbing Phase 3 depends on, proven end to end
